props.title: Lenny
props.initialSlug: Dustin Hoffman as groundbreaking, tragic comic Lenny Bruce

sections.content: Lenny (1974) stands as Bob Fosse's raw, uncompromising portrait of groundbreaking comedian Lenny Bruce, with Dustin Hoffman delivering a tour-de-force performance that captures Bruce's rapid evolution from nightclub hack to counter-cultural prophet. Shot in stark black and white by Bruce Surtees (who also photographed Dirty Harry (1971)), the film's documentary-style approach and non-linear structure revolutionized the biopic format, influencing later works like The People vs. Larry Flynt (1996) and Man on the Moon (1999). Fosse's background in choreography shows in the rhythmic editing between past and present, comedy and tragedy.

sections.content: The film's exploration of censorship and artistic freedom resonates strongly with other provocative comedic biopics. Richard Pryor: Live in Concert (1979) showed the raw power of boundary-pushing standup, while The King of Comedy (1982) examined the darker psychological aspects of comedy. Hoffman's immersive performance style, switching between Bruce's stage persona and private struggles, established a template followed by later comedian biopics like Man on the Moon (1999) with Jim Carrey as Andy Kaufman.

Fosse's decision to frame Bruce's story through the testimonies of his wife, mother, and agent creates a Citizen Kane (1941)-like structure that questions the nature of truth and memory. The film's frank depiction of drug use, explicit language, and sexual content pushed boundaries for 1974, earning an X rating initially. This confrontational approach mirrors Bruce's own battles with obscenity laws and social conventions, making the film both a biography and a continuation of his fight for free expression. sections.content: Lenny revolutionized how films depict comedy as a vehicle for social change. Bruce's evolution from conventional joke-teller to satirical commentator influenced generations of comedians and their cinematic portrayals. Films like The People vs. Larry Flynt (1996) and Good Night, and Good Luck (2005) continued exploring how controversial figures challenge societal norms through media. Fosse's film shows Bruce not just performing comedy but weaponizing it against hypocrisy and injustice.
